title: A follower that drops a conflicting previous entry at once, proved safe
summary: A Raft follower that holds an entry of another term at the index before the entries a leader sends refuses the request and keeps the entry: the leader backs up, sends from one entry earlier, and the conflicting entry is replaced then. A developer has the follower drop the conflicting entry and everything after it the moment it refuses, so that the leader's next try finds the index free. The contract's eight rows change from a rejection to a transition that truncates, the model's `Replicate` carries the truncation out and backs the leader up as before, and TLC checks the rule under all three configurations: log matching, leader completeness and state machine safety hold in 19,844, 8,578 and 14,244 states, no committed entry is ever overwritten, the followers still catch up and learn every commit under fairness, and six of the eight changed rows are taken, the two left being for an entry the follower already holds, which a one-step RPC never sends.

change.description: In `AppendRule.decide`, the `CONFLICTING` arm changes from `rejected` to `transition(MISSING, TRUNCATE)`, with the comment that the conflicting entry and everything after it are dropped now so that the leader's next try finds the index free; the rule's Javadoc says that `MISSING` is what it returns once it has done so, and that the leader backs up on anything but a match. The test that such a request is refused becomes one that it truncates. `CommitRule`, `RoleMachine` and `VoteRule` are untouched.

risk: Low, and the question a reviewer asks is whether an entry a follower drops on its own, before the leader has sent anything for its index, can be one that was committed: the follower does not know, and the paper's proof that it cannot be goes through leader completeness. The model has every run of three configurations with the rule as patched, and the figure 8 one is the configuration in which a leader of a later term overwrites what a stale one holds.
explanation: The append rule in the model is generated from the regenerated contract, so `Replicate` does what the eight patched rows say: on a transition with `TRUNCATE` and no `APPEND` the follower's log is cut to the entry before the conflicting one, and the rule's `MISSING` is no match, so the leader backs its next index up by one as it did on the rejection. Under the first configuration, 19,844 states, the second, 8,578, and the third, 14,244 under the fairness conditions, `LogMatching`, `LeaderCompleteness` and `StateMachineSafety` hold, and so does `CommittedEntriesNeverChange` on every step: the entry a follower drops is one at an index where the leader of a term no earlier than the follower's own holds a different entry, so by leader completeness it was never committed, and dropping it changes nothing a server has applied. The coverage shows six of the eight rows taken, with the entry sent absent or conflicting under the first configuration and as a heartbeat under all three, and the leader's next try landing on the `MISSING` rows, which refuse it as before; the two rows for an entry the follower already holds are ones no step takes, as under the committed rule, since an RPC that is one step is never duplicated or retried. The fourth configuration, with replies delayed and requests sent again, takes the rows for an entry the follower already holds, but with one entry per leader never a conflicting previous entry, so none of the eight; it verifies the change in 261,060 states, as many as the committed rule's.
resolution: Merge. The truncation is one the committed rule performs a round trip later, when the leader's next try finds the previous entry matching and the entry sent conflicting, and doing it at once is safe by the same argument; the proof is leader completeness, which the model checks with the rule as changed. The rows are checked under all three configurations on every build, and the third says that a follower which drops entries on its own still catches up and still learns every commit.
provenance: Constructed as the third example of the Raft replication model, to pair with 096 and 097: a change to the same rows as 096, correct this time, accepted on the strength of all three configurations and the coverage that shows the rows taken.

references.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (extended version, 2014): section 5.3, log replication and the consistency check; section 5.4, the election restriction, committing entries from previous terms, and figure 8
Ongaro, Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice (2014): chapter 3, the log matching, leader completeness and state machine safety properties and their proof
Ongaro, the TLA+ specification of Raft (raft.tla): AppendEntries, HandleAppendEntriesRequest and AdvanceCommitIndex, the actions this model's Replicate and AdvanceCommit stand for
